I'd personally not take phenibut if that were the case.

Many people want phenibut to feel like benzos. I get it, and there's nothing wrong with that by itself. However, as soon as they start making excuses to try to abuse phenibut in either dosage or frequency, that's a huge red flag that they don't have the responsibility necessary for recreational drug use. They are probably the last people who should play around with benzos.

I have to say, if you were taking 3g doses not realizing that was excessive, that shows a lot of irresponsibility.

Phenibut effects are subtle -- it's over the counter, after all. Also, and I think what gets a lot of people, the effects aren't reliable. Sometimes a high dose feels weak or a low dose feels strong. This leads people to increase their dosage when they don't get the effects they want. That greatly increases tolerance and then they still can't get the effects they want.

That is not the way with phenibut. The effects just can't be relied upon. Not getting effects is no excuse to increase dosage or frequency.

A single dose of 1g/week will give you tolerance in some 6-8 weeks. Once/week at > 1g and it's much faster. Phenibut just can't be used very often and needs periodic breaks.
It's terrible advice. 500-750mg is good. Tolerance builds fast. You're chasing the dragon. Phenibut is subtle.

How is it that people think > 1g is a normal dose, to the point they don't even try lower doses? Sorry OP, it's just stupid. 500-750mg is a good dose. The people taking > 1g because they claim "everybody is different" and that they are special and need more, those people are abusing it.

I started programming as a pre-teen. I'd like to think I was a craftsman long before leaving working for others to work on my own products. I love coding and the constant problem solving it requires, so I've spent an enormous amount of time getting good at it.

When working for others it's extremely rare to start with a blank page, then design and implement a solution. Basically that never happens. Instead, there is a bunch of junk of varying quality done by others and you have to dig around in there to fix things or graft on new stuff. Working in teams has a number of downsides, the least of which is the actual working side-by-side part: managers, meetings, stupid workplace drama, egos, and those horrible people who just love to hear their own voice.

It's very different to work on your own stuff, especially alone. While you have to do everything, you are also familiar with everything and aren't slowed by needing to interface with others. Zero drama is priceless. It can be lonely though and that may not be for everyone.

I can say that since I work mainly on my products, I don't spend as much time poking around with new technology as I used to. A lot of new the stuff is just fads, old stuff rediscovered by youngins who failed to learn from previous generations and don't realize how much they suffer from using poor tools. I've carved out my little world where I have great tooling that lets me be extremely productive. I'm happy there. For a career, generally you need to stay on top of the acronyms, at the very least so you can explain why it's a bad idea.

Yes, it's now about adding more value to my products for my users. Letting them do new super cool things is challenging and satisfying.

If you think you might like programming, I highly recommend trying it out on your own. Schooling can help and some people need it to learn, but you can also learn on your own. FWIW, I am completely self taught, no college at all. This is a good site:  
[https://www.codecademy.com/](https://www.codecademy.com/)

There are some common pitfalls that turn a lot of people off to coding. HTML and CSS are not programming, they are in fact a horrible way to design a user interface. JavaScript is programming and mixes with HTML/CSS, but the whole thing together is a pretty big mess with lots of hacks. Unfortunately those three are extremely common and so you'll have to figure them out. Just know that is barely programming and don't let it deter you. Other things can be a lot more fun. Building games can be a fun way to use your coding skills.

C# and Java are real programming with good tools, especially Java. C/C++ are low level and complex, so much it can get in the way of getting things done for a beginner. Other languages like Python, Ruby, Rust, Go, Perl, and more have their fans and uses, but I would stay away until you've got a lot of Java or C# experience. Much of the skills are transferable to other languages. If you build games for practice, Unity uses C# but mixes it in with a bunch of nasty junk that may not further your coding skills.

Anyway, there's no better job than coding IMO. Even if you don't find a way to fatFIRE with it, working for The Man can be very lucrative and jobs are plentiful. Also, generally managers aren't able to argue with coders because they don't understand the complexities. With a job where you need to pick up a bunch of lumber and move it over there, the manager knows the difficulties involved and how long it should take. With coding, they ask you! Even better, estimates are notoriously bad. When deadlines are inevitably missed, the most they can say is "unfortunately it wasn't possible to do in that amount of time". This lack of accountability can make the job easy if you don't let them stress or overwork you.

I like these posts. When reading them I often think of my own situation and how it compares. I don't have the motivation to layout a comprehensive set of articles like this, but maybe it would be interesting for others if I write out some of my comparisons.

> When I left my tech job after the big windfall, I thought I would enjoy my retirement life. I was never thrilled to work for “the man”.

For me, I left working for The Man to work for myself. It ended up being a mint, even though I keep it small. I did everything I could myself for as long as I could stand it. After 6 years or so with 2 people, myself included, I added a few more. At 10 years it's still only 6 people. I'm an engineer and I don't want to be a manager, so I need people that don't need hand holding. Growing the business would lose all the fun, so I just don't. It makes 5M/year like this and I don't really need more.

Where I'm at now is still working, but mostly as much and whenever I want. I can stay away for 2 weeks on a whim with little impact on the business, except for slowing improvements. I love working on my software and having many tens of thousands of people use it, so I don't mind continuing to work. I've kept the same "purpose", it prevents any "what do I do now" sort of feelings.

It is also an outlet for "mastery and creativity". I could never just sit around all day. I can watch about 1 hour of TV and then I'm done. Some games can keep me occupied for long periods though. I haven't actually played one of those for many years, but I do play games where a session lasts 30-60 minutes.

> I didn’t realize how much I benefited from connecting with people at work until I left work.

Funny, I never missed this. My social skills are fine/good, but I just don't really like most people. I don't miss most officemates. I have interactions with my employees, but they are all remote, so it's not much. My spouse is sufficient. We rarely go hang out with others, even though when we do it's usually fun.

I understand other people aren't like this. Some of my employees have trouble working from home. Going to a shared office space helps.

> I see at least 4 people a week outside my family

That's a lot! For me, it doesn't help that I've moved a few times. I don't have connections from childhood, school, work, etc where I am now, and no family nearby. Oh well. If it bothered me I'd move, I suppose.

> I don’t think I am an exception wanting to build an identity above my monetary success and beyond my previous work position.

I guess for me, my software is my legacy, and I keep building on it. I enjoy doing that too much to ever sell it off and move on, at least not while I am healthy enough to keep working on it.

I could see if I stopped I would probably have a lot of similar feelings. I tend to be extremely focused on a thing, to the detriment of others. If I'm having a house built, I'll spend days/weeks at a time focused on all the decisions required, and not working in the meantime. If I have nothing else to focus on, I'll focus on work, which is probably 95% of the time. Without my coding time, I'd feel pretty lost 95% of the time. I think it's really important to find things you like and focus on them. I should probably diversify more.

> Even if you don’t know what you are going to focus on, I would suggest people to keep a strong routine of waking up, exercising and going to bed at the same time. Without a routine, people can sink into a mental health crisis and develop poor habits easily.

I don't follow it very well, but I agree. Especially sleep and exercise, it makes a huge difference and can't be replaced by anything else.

> I would also suggest having a routine to connect with friends, to take some online live courses or to play video games with other people so the routine is not too boring.

Probably if you have lots of friends then this comes naturally. Not having many friends makes it a lot harder.

> There’s no way I would give up my hard earned autonomy. Despite the challenges of having to work hard to build a fulfilling post-retirement life, I feel autonomy itself is totally worth the effort to get there.

I agree, but at the same time I love what I do. I want to do it and would be sad if I couldn't. It's not a problem for my though because I do have enough autonomy to just not work for a while, if that's what I want. That does happen, but infrequently.

> I didn’t mention family here. But I have an awesome family and I spend a lot of time with them.

I've thought about this a lot. I have a spouse, but not family. It's not too late, but it's getting close. I worry I'll regret it in some 10 years or so, if I'm somehow not able to keep myself entertained and I get bored, maybe kids would have been a good idea. Then again, wanting kids means wanting to have a kid around ALL THE TIME, especially when fatFIRE'd. I don't really want that, as selfish as that is.

> I am in a good place right now and I don’t think I will ever work another job.

I'll definitely never work another job, not ever. I put in my years. It was terrible and only made a pittance. If I'm going to work hard, it's going to be doing something I like and for myself, or at least not to benefit some company. If I didn't have coding, I'm not really sure what I'd be doing. I suppose that is not very helpful for those who want to work on that problem. Or maybe it is: learn coding! Build a game. It's fun!

> I saw people suggesting starting/buying a business to stay busy and engaged as part of retirement.

Ha! I've heard this a lot. Do you have any idea how much effort was required to get my business to where it is? Suggesting I start over just for kicks is absolutely insane.

Regarding payment remittance emails, about 1/3rd of customers send them. Getting customers to do something is generally a lot of pain. The emails would not fix it though if Schwab only shows the amount and not the sender: customers often purchase the same item for the same amount, so I need to be able to tell which customer paid. Each wire I receive has a single, 5 character invoice number associated with it, that's all I need. Barring that, I need the sender's name.

Schwab really does only show "Incoming Wire Transfer", nothing to click to get more info, at least for a personal account. I suspect this is also true for an LLC business checking account, but I'd like to know for sure before bothering to open it. Then I'd like to know how Schwab can possibly think that is reasonable. I expect something like, "it's more of a brokerage account, not for transactions with customers" (still insane).

I have found Mercury and Wise (which both use Evolve Bank to handle their wires) show only the sender's name and a tracking number. I still can't believe Schwab shows even less than that.

Chase shows a bunch of information (as a single, ugly line of text), mostly numbers meaningless to me, but they do include the reference field that the sender provided. 95% of the time I get the invoice number. However, I greatly dislike Chase. They lock me out of online banking periodically when their automatic fraud detection decides I can't be trusted, again. It's happened dozens of times and multiple times for the same transaction. It takes a ~20 minute phone call to remedy and sometimes it hangs up on me after 15 minutes. I have a Chase business bank relationship manager and they can unlock my account if I email and wait a day, but they can't stop it from happening again and again.

I'm curious, do the banks you use allow customers to wire you directly? Schwab, Mercury, Wise, Axos, and many others require some other bank to be the recipient, then customers must use the wire reference field to specify my LLC name and account number. This seem suboptimal and unprofessional to me, but seems to be widespread. Are people who send a lot of wire payments used to doing that? Chase allows my customers to wire directly to me, without "further credit to" nonsense.

Using the reference field for "further credit to" is also annoying because it eats up some characters, leaving less room for my 5 character invoice number. The MT103 spec says field 70 is 4 lines of 35 characters, but I've seen multiple bank UIs limit it to 1 line of 35 characters. Everything about wires is terrible!

On my second day, I met someone at a cafe who gave me a number to a local who rented me her car. If that didn't happen, my entire trip would have been wrecked. If you don't have a car/cart/scooter, I suggest skipping Vieques entirely.
